claims.text: A PVD coating comprising alternating TiN and TiB2 layers with a thermal-expansion-matching interlayer can be deposited on bulk CoCrFeNi.
The modified multilayer coating will maintain low friction from room temperature to 800 °C.
The modified multilayer coating will reduce wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi.
A tailored interlayer will mitigate thermal-expansion mismatch between the ceramic multilayer and the CoCrFeNi substrate.
The interlayer will help the multilayer remain adherent and intact during thermal cycling.
Sliding at elevated temperature will promote formation of a self-adaptive tribo-oxide film on the coating.
At lower temperatures, dense TiN/TiB2 layers will prevent direct metal-to-metal contact by acting as a physical barrier.
At elevated temperatures, controlled oxidation of the coating will form TiO2 or composite oxide phases.
The coating-derived oxide phases will be lubricious and form a low-shear tribofilm.
A dense oxide or glaze layer can provide better high-temperature surface protection than a loose, mechanically unstable oxide layer.
The multilayer architecture and interlayer will manage thermal stresses and preserve coating adhesion.
Preserving coating adhesion while generating a low-shear oxide film will produce stable friction and wear performance over the full temperature range.
Uncoated CoCrFeNi typically exhibits increasing friction with increasing temperature.
Uncoated CoCrFeNi typically exhibits increasing wear with increasing temperature.
The proposed operating range is ambient air, room temperature to 800 °C, and normal loads of 10–20 N.
Successful performance depends on avoiding coating delamination caused by thermal mismatch.
Successful performance depends on reproducible, controlled oxidation kinetics during sliding.
Failure to achieve statistically significant reductions in both mean friction coefficient and wear rate, or occurrence of coating delamination, would falsify the hypothesis.
